text:
Keep the Loops

Every few years, a new round of enthusiasm arrives for abandoning joined-up handwriting in primary schools. Keyboards are everywhere, the argument goes, so why spend precious hours teaching children to link their letters? I think this is a mistake. Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, and they should teach it well. The case does not rest on nostalgia. It rests on what we know about how children learn, what handwriting does for the mind, and what a school owes to every child, including those who will never own a laptop they can rely on.

Start with the honest version of the opposing view, because it has real force. Time in a primary school day is scarce. Reading, mathematics, science, art, music and play all compete for it. Cursive, or joined writing, takes many hours of practice to learn, and many adults never write it in a way that looks like the models in the workbooks. Most of us end up with a personal hybrid of print and joins. Meanwhile, nearly all of the writing children will do as adults will happen on screens. If the aim of school is to prepare children for the world they will live in, shouldn't typing take priority?

The trouble is that this argument treats handwriting as only a means of getting words onto a surface. It is more than that, and the research on what it is more than is hard to ignore.

Consider first what happens in a child's brain when they write by hand. Studies using brain imaging have found that handwriting activates networks involved in reading and in memory more strongly than typing does. Forming a letter requires the hand to produce a shape that is different every time and that the child must control. Pressing a key requires no such thing. Every letter on a keyboard is the same press of a finger, differing only in location. Researchers have compared children who learned letters by writing them with children who learned them by typing, and the handwriters tended to recognise letters more reliably and to read more fluently. This makes intuitive sense. The motion of making a shape helps fix the shape in memory. The child who has drawn a letter a hundred times knows it in a way the child who has pressed it a hundred times may not.

Notice that this finding supports handwriting in general, and a sceptic could say it supports print as well as cursive. That is fair, and it brings me to the heart of the matter. Why joined-up specifically?

The first answer is fluency. When a child prints, the pen lifts from the page after every letter. Each lift is a small interruption, and each new start must be aimed. Joined writing turns a word into a single movement. The hand develops rhythm, and the child can think about what to say rather than where to put the next stroke. Teachers who have watched children move from print to a joined style often report that speed rises and that the writing becomes more comfortable over long stretches. This matters most in the years when children are asked to write more, such as in upper primary and into secondary school, when exams demand sustained writing against a clock. A child who has never learned an efficient, joined hand is at a disadvantage precisely when the stakes rise.

The second answer concerns spelling. A joined word is learned as a pattern of movement. Letter strings that recur in English, such as the endings in "tion" or "ing", become physical habits of the hand. Many teachers argue that this muscle memory helps children spell, because the hand supports the memory of the word. The evidence here is less settled than the case for handwriting in general, and I will not claim more for it than it deserves. But the logic is plausible, and it matches what many experienced classroom teachers have seen over decades.

The third answer is about children who find literacy hard. Children with dyslexia and related difficulties often struggle with reversing letters, particularly b and d. In print these two letters are mirror images, one a ball on the left and the other a ball on the right. In a joined style taught with proper entry strokes, they begin differently, and the join itself gives the hand a cue. Specialists in this area have long recommended cursive for many of these learners, precisely because the continuous movement and the distinct starting points reduce confusion. If a school drops joined writing altogether, it may take away a tool that helps the very children who most need support.

A fourth answer is about equality. The argument that "everyone will type" assumes that every child will have easy and reliable access to a keyboard, at school and at home, and the skill to use it. That is not true now and will not be true for some time. Children from poorer households may have less access to devices outside school. A school that teaches handwriting well gives every child the same basic technology, one that costs a pencil and a sheet of paper and never runs out of battery. Dropping the teaching of a skill does not make it unnecessary. It makes it a skill that families with time and money will teach privately, and those without will not. We have seen this pattern before in education, and it widens gaps rather than closing them.

There is also a practical point about the present. Children will be handwriting for years to come. They write in exercise books, in tests, in note-taking, on forms and in countless small moments of adult life, from shopping lists to birthday cards. Examinations in many countries are still handwritten, and examiners still cannot read what they cannot decipher. A child who writes slowly and illegibly loses marks, whatever the quality of their ideas. Teaching a fast, legible hand is therefore not a luxury. It is a basic form of access to being understood.

Then there is the matter of what we lose culturally, which I raise last and with some caution, because it is the weakest part of the case on its own. Joined writing is how most of our history was recorded. Letters, diaries, wills and registers are in it. A generation that cannot read cursive cannot read its great-grandparents' letters, or the marginal notes in a family Bible, without a translator. That is a real loss, even if it is not the strongest reason to keep teaching the skill. Reading cursive is easier once you have learned to write it.

What would good teaching look like? Here I want to be clear that I am not defending the way it was sometimes done in the past, with rigid drills, rulers across knuckles and penalties for left-handers. The case for joined-up handwriting is a case for teaching it sensibly. Children should learn to form letters correctly in print first, in the early years, because this is the foundation for both reading and writing. Joins should be introduced once letter formation is secure, typically around the age of seven. Lessons should be short and frequent, because ten minutes of focused practice most days beats an hour once a week. Left-handed children should be taught with attention to their paper position and grip. And no child should be shamed for a style that is legible and fluent but not identical to the model. The goal is a hand that is quick, clear and comfortable, not a copy of a copperplate sample.

Typing should be taught too. This is not a contest between two skills in which only one can survive. Children need both, and a good primary curriculum has room for both. A child who can write fluently by hand and type competently is better prepared than one who can only do the second. If time is the problem, the answer is to protect a small, steady amount of it for handwriting, not to remove it. Fifteen minutes a day across six years is modest in a curriculum, and the return on it is substantial.

Some will say that the evidence is not conclusive, and they are right that some of the research is mixed and that more is needed. But the burden of proof should sit with the change. Handwriting has been taught for centuries, the existing evidence mostly points in its favour, and the downsides of keeping it are small. The downsides of abandoning it, if the research on reading, fluency and support for struggling learners is even partly right, could be large and would fall hardest on the children least able to compensate. When the costs of being wrong are lopsided in this way, caution is the sensible course.

So the answer to the question is yes. Primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. They should teach it early enough to be useful, gently enough to be enjoyed, and briefly enough to leave room for everything else. They should do so because it helps children learn letters, write at speed, spell with confidence and cope with difficulty, and because a pencil and paper remain the fairest technology a school can hand to a child. The loops and links are small things. They are worth keeping.
